Mechanics papers in this field rarely say "the brain". They say "the E10.5 neuroepithelium", "the ventricular zone" or "the cortical plate", and the age and the layer matter as much as the number. For example, mouse embryos lacking the mechanosensitive channel Piezo1 have, at E10.5, a thinner neuroepithelium in the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain [@nourse2022piezo, Results; Fig. 1]. This chapter gives you the map and the clock needed to read such sentences.

::: {.callout-note title="After this chapter you will be able to"}
- name the zones of the developing cortical wall, from the ventricle to the pial surface, and say which cells live in each;
- describe how neuroepithelial cells give rise to radial glia and basal progenitors, and when this happens in the mouse;
- place key mouse events on an embryonic (E) and postnatal (P) timeline, and refuse to transfer ages between species;
- list the staging ages of the Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas.
:::

## Ages, stages and species {#sec-anatomy-ages}

Mouse ages are written as embryonic days (E) and postnatal days (P). In the Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas, E11.5 means 11.5 days post conception, and P0 is the day of birth [@thompson2014high, Experimental Procedures, sec. "ISH"]. Nourse and colleagues count the day of vaginal plug observation as E0.5 [@nourse2022piezo, Methods].

An E-day is a stage of one species only: rat E12 is not mouse E12 (a course convention, not a claim from a source). Human fetal tissue is staged in gestation weeks (GW), not E-days [@long2019extracellular, sec. 4.2, pp. 7–8]. This chapter therefore uses mouse data for mouse ages, and keeps other species in clearly labelled places.

## From neural plate to neural tube {#sec-anatomy-tube}

The brain starts as a sheet. The **neural plate** is "the neuroectodermal epithelium before the formation of the neural groove and neural tube"; the **neural tube** is the same epithelium after the groove has closed [@gotz2005cell, p. 779, glossary]. In the mouse, neural tube formation takes place around E9.5 [@long2019extracellular, sec. 2.1.2, p. 3]. By E10.5 the tube has closed and consists mainly of neural stem cells and nascent neurons [@nourse2022piezo, Results].

Brain regions develop from back to front: hindbrain, then midbrain, then forebrain [@nourse2022piezo, Results]. The most anterior part is the **telencephalon**, which includes the cerebral cortex [@gotz2005cell, p. 780, glossary]. In the mouse hindbrain, cells are born in transient compartments called **rhombomeres**, which cannot exchange cells until their borders disappear; the hindbrain is segmented between E8.5 and E11.5 [@moody2005ion, p. 897].

The Allen atlas describes the whole tube with the **prosomeric model**. It cuts the tube lengthwise into four longitudinal plates (roof, alar, basal, floor), and crosswise into segments called neuromeres [@thompson2014high, Results, secs. "New Developmental Reference Atlases" and "Molecular principles"]. At E11.5, gene expression groups brain structures mainly by plate. Between E15.5 and E18.5, identity switches to an areal organisation [@thompson2014high, Results, sec. "Molecular principles of brain organization"].

## The neuroepithelium and its progenitors {#sec-anatomy-progenitors}

The wall of the early tube is a **neuroepithelium**: a single layer of cells that spans the whole wall, from the inner (apical) surface facing the ventricle to the outer (basal) surface, which rests on a basal lamina [@gotz2005cell, pp. 777–778]. It looks multilayered (**pseudostratified**) only because the nuclei move during the cell cycle. This **interkinetic nuclear migration** carries the nucleus basally for S phase and back to the apical surface for mitosis [@gotz2005cell, p. 779, glossary; p. 783]. The layer lining the ventricle that contains most progenitor cell bodies is the **ventricular zone (VZ)** [@gotz2005cell, p. 778].

At first, neuroepithelial cells divide symmetrically and multiply. Later they divide asymmetrically, into one copy of themselves plus a neuron or a progenitor [@gotz2005cell, p. 777; Fig. 1]. With the onset of neurogenesis they turn into **radial glial cells**. These keep their apical and basal contacts but lose tight junctions and gain astroglial markers. In mice, this happens in most of the brain between E10 and E12 [@gotz2005cell, p. 778; Table 1].

**Apical radial glia (aRG)** are attached to both surfaces: their apical process to the ventricular surface, and their basal endfeet to the pial basement membrane [@long2019extracellular, sec. 2.3.1, pp. 4–5]. **Basal radial glia (bRG)** sit further out and lack the apical process [@long2019extracellular, sec. 2.3.1, p. 5]. **Basal progenitors** retract their apical process and divide at the basal side of the VZ, or in the **subventricular zone (SVZ)**. The SVZ is a mitotic layer basal to the VZ, most prominent in the telencephalon. Basal progenitors often divide into two neurons [@gotz2005cell, p. 779].

These progenitors are also electrically active, which links this chapter to @sec-membrane. In mouse, all VZ cells express delayed K⁺ currents at E12–E14, and a subset expresses Na⁺ currents from E14 [@moody2005ion, p. 895].

## The cortical wall at mid-neurogenesis {#sec-anatomy-wall}

Newborn neurons leave the germinal zones and migrate outwards. They move along radial glial processes up to the **cortical plate**, the layer where they settle (**locomotion**). At the end they detach and move quickly on their own (**terminal translocation**) [@long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2, p. 6]. Outside the cortical plate lies the **marginal zone**, where **Cajal–Retzius cells** secrete reelin, a glycoprotein needed for normal migration and layering [@long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2, p. 6]. @fig-anatomy-wall puts these zones together.

**Schematic, not data.** Not to scale: the mouse cortical wall during neurogenesis, ventricle at the bottom and pial surface at the top. Lines: radial glial processes ending in basal endfeet at the pial basement membrane. Blue: apical radial glia, nuclei drawn at different heights because of interkinetic nuclear migration. Green: basal progenitors and a basal radial glial cell in the SVZ. Grey: neurons migrating outwards along radial glia. Orange: neurons in the cortical plate. Purple: a Cajal–Retzius cell in the marginal zone. Hover over cells for labels. Zone names and cell types are from @gotz2005cell [pp. 778–779; Fig. 2] and @long2019extracellular [secs. 2.3.1 and 3.2]. The zone between the SVZ and the cortical plate is left unnamed because none of the course sources defines it. Illustrative; no thicknesses or cell numbers are implied.
:::

The extracellular matrix (ECM) anchors this wall. If integrin β1 is knocked out in the mouse neocortex at E11, radial glial processes detach from the basal surface within 24 h [@long2019extracellular, Fig. 1d, p. 4]. At E14.5, laminin α2 and α4 are high in the VZ, and integrin α6β1 is enriched along the ventricular surface [@long2019extracellular, sec. 2.1.2, p. 3]. @sec-ecm describes these molecules.

The cerebral cortex forms as a smooth sheet. In some species it stays smooth (**lissencephalic**); in others it folds (**gyrencephalic**) [@vanessen1997tension, p. 314]. The proliferative capacity of basal progenitors is thought to be partly responsible for the evolutionary expansion of the neocortex. Ferrets have more proliferative basal progenitors than mice, and a more expanded and folded neocortex [@long2019extracellular, sec. 2.1.2, p. 3].

::: {.callout-note title="Human comparison (gestation weeks, not E-days)"}
In human fetal neocortex, physiological folding has begun by 22 GW. In explants at 11–16 GW, before physiological folding, adding the ECM components HAPLN1, lumican and collagen I induced folding of the cortical plate within 24 h [@long2019extracellular, sec. 4.2, pp. 7–8]. These ages cannot be converted to mouse E-days.
:::

## A timeline of mouse brain development {#sec-anatomy-timeline}

@fig-anatomy-timeline collects the mouse ages from this chapter on one axis. Click an event (or tab to it and press Enter) to see what happens and the source. Events close in age overlap; Tab steps through them one by one.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-anatomy-timeline
//| fig-cap: "**Data/values from** @moody2005ion, @long2019extracellular, @gotz2005cell, @nourse2022piezo, @thompson2014high and @fawcett2019roles. Selected events in mouse brain development, on an axis with separate embryonic (E0–E19) and postnatal (P0–P28) segments. Dots are single ages; bars are periods. Every event is quoted from its source with species and age as stated there: Moody & Bosma 2005 (hindbrain segmentation, ventricular-zone cells), Long & Huttner 2019 (neural tube, laminins, marginal zone), Götz & Huttner 2005 (radial glia transition), Nourse et al. 2022 (E10.5 neuroepithelium), Thompson et al. 2014 (atlas stages, organisation, eye opening, myelin genes) and Fawcett et al. 2019 (perineuronal nets, reported for mice and rats). No values were read off figures. The positions of events are exact; the axis has no gestation length, so the birth break is not to scale."
viewof anatEvent = anatTimeline(anatEvents, {
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  colors: { mouse: "#2a78d6" },
  eMax: 19, pMax: 28,
  note: "Mouse only. Ages from other species (rat, human gestation weeks) are not placed on this axis."
})
```

Three points are easy to miss:

- **Neurogenesis follows a schedule per region.** A schematic for rodents in @gotz2005cell [Fig. 3, p. 780] shows telencephalic neurogenesis from approx. E10.5 to approx. E17.5, with a peak near approx. E14. These are readings from a schematic and are not on the timeline.
- **Ion channels come late.** Ion-channel and G-protein-coupled-receptor genes are mostly switched on late in development, and neurotransmitter and ion-channel genes show very low expression at E13.5 across all brain regions [@thompson2014high, Results, sec. "Mapping gene expression"; Fig. S1 legend].
- **The adult reference lies off the axis.** The atlas's postnatal stages are P4, P14 and P28, and P56 serves as the adult reference [@thompson2014high, Introduction].

Perineuronal nets, the ECM structures of @sec-ecm, appear only after about P23 in mice and rats [@fawcett2019roles, p. 453].

## The embryonic brain in 3D {#sec-anatomy-3d}

Sections and timelines flatten an organ that grows in three dimensions. The viewer below shows the embryonic mouse brain as 3D surfaces, so that you can turn the regions named in this chapter and see how they sit relative to each other. Its meshes come from a reference atlas, not from the papers this course is built on, and they are credited separately in the viewer.

```{ojs}

Use it to see where regions sit, not as evidence for any claim in this chapter. Region groups (pallium, subpallium, hypothalamus and preoptic area, diencephalon, midbrain, hindbrain, ventricles) follow the atlas ontology.

## Check yourself {#sec-anatomy-check}

:::{.qmulti correct="4"}
Going from the ventricle outwards, which order of zones is correct in the developing mouse cortex?

- ventricular zone → cortical plate → subventricular zone → marginal zone

  > The subventricular zone is basal to the ventricular zone [@gotz2005cell, p. 779]; the cortical plate, where migrating neurons settle, is further out [@long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2, p. 6].

- subventricular zone → ventricular zone → cortical plate → marginal zone

  > The ventricular zone is the layer that lines the ventricle [@gotz2005cell, p. 778]; the subventricular zone is basal to it [@gotz2005cell, p. 779].

- ventricular zone → subventricular zone → marginal zone → cortical plate

  > The marginal zone lies outside the cortical plate, at the pial side [@long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2, p. 6].

- ventricular zone → subventricular zone → cortical plate → marginal zone

  > Correct [@gotz2005cell, pp. 778–779; @long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2].

:::

:::{.qmulti correct="1"}
When do neuroepithelial cells turn into radial glial cells in most of the mouse brain?

- Between E10 and E12.

  > Correct: at E10 no astroglial markers are detectable yet, and by E12 the transition has occurred [@gotz2005cell, p. 778].

- Between E8.5 and E11.5.

  > That is when the mouse hindbrain is segmented into rhombomeres [@moody2005ion, p. 897].

- Between E9.5 and E10.5.

  > In this window the neural tube forms and closes [@long2019extracellular, sec. 2.1.2, p. 3; @nourse2022piezo, Results]; at E10 no astroglial markers are detectable yet [@gotz2005cell, p. 778].

- Between E15.5 and E18.5.

  > That is when regional identity switches from plate-based to areal organisation in the Allen atlas [@thompson2014high, Results, sec. "Molecular principles of brain organization"].

:::

**Compute.** For how many days is the mouse hindbrain segmented into rhombomeres? {{< qinput 3 tol=0 hints="From E8.5 to E11.5" >}} days [@moody2005ion, p. 897].

:::{.qmulti correct="4"}
A paper reports an effect in rat cortex at E14. Where does it go on the mouse timeline of this chapter?

- At mouse E14, because rodents develop on the same schedule.

  > The course sources do not support transferring ages between species, and the timeline widget warns about it.

- At mouse E12, two days earlier, to allow for the species gap.

  > No course source gives a conversion between rat and mouse E-days, so any shift would be invented.

- At mouse E14.5, because mouse ages are counted from E0.5.

  > The plug day is counted as E0.5 in mouse papers [@nourse2022piezo, Methods]. That fixes how days are counted, not how a rat age maps onto a mouse age.

- Off the mouse axis, reported separately as a result from rat E14.

  > Correct. E-days are specific to each species, so a rat E14 is not a mouse E14. That is why the timeline shows a mouse lane only.

:::

:::{.qmulti correct="1"}
Where do basal progenitors divide?

- At the basal side of the ventricular zone, or within the subventricular zone.

  > Correct; they often divide into two neurons [@gotz2005cell, p. 779].

- At the apical surface of the ventricular zone, like neuroepithelial cells.

  > Neuroepithelial cells move the nucleus back to the apical surface for mitosis [@gotz2005cell, p. 783], but basal progenitors retract their apical process [@gotz2005cell, p. 779].

- In the cortical plate, among neurons that have finished migrating.

  > The cortical plate is where migrating neurons settle [@long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2, p. 6]; the mitotic layers are the ventricular and subventricular zones [@gotz2005cell, p. 779].

- In the marginal zone, alongside the reelin-secreting Cajal–Retzius cells.

  > The marginal zone holds the Cajal–Retzius cells, which secrete reelin [@long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2, p. 6]; it is not where progenitors divide [@gotz2005cell, p. 779].

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answers" collapse="true"}
1. VZ → SVZ → cortical plate → marginal zone [@gotz2005cell, pp. 778–779; @long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2, p. 6].
2. E10–E12 [@gotz2005cell, p. 778].
3. 3 days, from E8.5 to E11.5 [@moody2005ion, p. 897].
4. Off the mouse axis, labelled as rat; ages are not transferred between species (rat E-days are not mouse E-days).
5. Basal side of the VZ or in the SVZ [@gotz2005cell, p. 779].
:::

## Summary {#sec-anatomy-summary}

- The mouse neural tube forms around E9.5 and is closed by E10.5. Its wall is then a pseudostratified neuroepithelium of stem cells and nascent neurons [@long2019extracellular, p. 3; @nourse2022piezo, Results].
- Neuroepithelial cells become radial glia between E10 and E12. Most neurons derive, directly or via basal progenitors, from radial glia [@gotz2005cell, pp. 778–779].
- Neurons migrate along radial glia to the cortical plate, below the marginal zone with its reelin-secreting Cajal–Retzius cells [@long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2, p. 6].
- The Allen developmental atlas stages are E11.5, E13.5, E15.5, E18.5, P4, P14 and P28, plus P56 [@thompson2014high, Introduction]. Ages are never transferred between species.

:::{.qflashcards}

- What is the ventricular zone?

  > The layer lining the ventricle that contains most progenitor cell bodies [@gotz2005cell, p. 778].

- What is interkinetic nuclear migration?

  > The movement of the nucleus away from the apical surface for S phase and back to it for mitosis, which makes the neuroepithelium look layered.

- How do basal radial glia differ from apical radial glia?

  > They lie more basally and lack the apical process to the ventricular surface [@long2019extracellular, sec. 2.3.1].

- What does the marginal zone contain?

  > Cajal–Retzius cells, which secrete reelin [@long2019extracellular, sec. 3.2].

:::
